questions.q: At a riverside site, one team member lifts out burnt grains and pieces of brick from under the soil, while another examines how the layers of soil and stone in the river bank were laid down. Which pair of specialists are they?
questions.a: An archaeologist and a geologist
o: An archaeologist and a geologist
A palaeontologist and an anthropologist
An anthropologist and a geologist
A palaeontologist and an archaeologist

questions.q: Tanvi claims: 'To write about our town in the last 30 years, a historian can use television and the internet; to write about a king of 1,500 years ago, she can use old newspapers.' Is Tanvi right? Explain using the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. She is right that for the last few decades electronic media such as television and the internet can be consulted. She is wrong about the king: newspapers are a source when historians study recent history, which usually means the last two or three centuries, so they do not exist for a king of 1,500 years ago; for him the historian must gather information from as many other sources as she can find.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: electronic media can be used for the last few decades
Wrong part: newspapers help only for recent history (last two or three centuries), not 1,500 years ago

questions.q:
Match each specialist in Column A with the piece of evidence in Column B that he or she would study.
Column A: 1. Geologist  2. Palaeontologist  3. Anthropologist  4. Epigraphist
Column B: a. writing engraved on an old copper plate  b. layers of stones and soil on a hillside  c. a fish preserved as an impression in rock  d. the customs of a village community today

Both palaeontologists and archaeologists can end up studying bones.
(a) A human tooth is found in the ashes of a hearth, among broken pots, at a village site lived in 3,000 years ago. Which of the two specialists should study it, and what clue decides it?
(b) The bones of an animal from millions of years ago are found preserved as an impression inside a layer of rock. Which specialist should study them, and what clue decides it?
questions.a: (a) An archaeologist: the tooth is among remains that people left behind at a site they lived in (hearth, pots), which archaeologists dig up and study. (b) A palaeontologist: the bones are from millions of years ago and are preserved in rock as a fossil, which is what palaeontologists study.
s: (a) Archaeologist, because the tooth lies among remains people left behind
(b) Palaeontologist, because the remains are a fossil from millions of years ago

questions.q:
At a dig beside a river in Telangana, the project board says: 'Aim: to learn how the people of this hamlet lived beside the river, and why they left it.' The team leader's list of finds reads:
P. The impression of a fish preserved in a slab of rock - archaeologist
Q. Clay beads and a broken pot - archaeologist
R. Lines of writing scratched on a copper plate - anthropologist
S. Layers of sand in the river bank showing that the river once flowed right past the huts and later moved away - no one yet
The copper plate has already been photographed, and the photographs have been sent to a university where its writing will be read next year.
(a) Find P is wrongly assigned. What is such a find called, and which specialist studies it?
(b) Find R is also wrongly assigned. Which specialist named in the chapter studies it?
(c) Which specialist named in the chapter studies finds like S, and what part of the aim could that work help with?
(d) Village elders tell a story that the people left the hamlet because of a great war. Suppose the study of S shows the river moved away at about the time the huts were left. Using the chapter's jigsaw idea, how should the team treat the two explanations, and what could help it decide?
questions.a: (a) A fossil (a preserved impression of an animal); a palaeontologist studies it. (b) An epigraphist, who studies ancient inscriptions. (c) A geologist, who studies physical features of the Earth such as soil, rivers and stones; the shifting river could help explain why the people left the hamlet. (d) The elders' story is an oral source and the river layers are another piece; if the pieces do not match, the team should not drop either at once but gather more sources (for example the copper plate's writing when it is read next year, or signs of burning or weapons at the site) and then decide which source it can trust more. Both causes could also be partly true.
s: (a) Fossil, studied by a palaeontologist
(b) Epigraphist, the specialist for ancient inscriptions
(c) Geologist (soil, rivers, stones), linked to why the people left
(d) Keeps both explanations, seeks more sources (such as the plate's reading or other finds) and then decides which to trust more

questions.q: A scientist tests the substances left inside pots dug up at an old site to find out what was cooked in them. In the chapter's words, she is making a ___ study of excavated materials.
questions.a: chemical

questions.q: Interpret why the chapter says that the past is studied 'not just by historians'. Give three reasons, each with an example of who else helps.
questions.a: (1) Some evidence lies in the ground and must be dug up: archaeologists excavate tools, pots, bones and burnt grains. (2) Some evidence needs special reading: epigraphists study ancient inscriptions, and experts in literature and languages read old texts. (3) Some questions need science: in the last 50 years, studies of ancient climates, chemical studies of excavated materials and genetics of ancient people have given fresh insights. Anthropologists also study human societies and cultures.
s: Reason 1 with an example such as archaeologists digging up remains
Reason 2 with an example such as epigraphists or language experts
Reason 3 with an example such as scientific studies of climate, chemistry or genetics

questions.q: A museum label reads 'Dug up by archaeologists'. Which object could NOT carry this label?
questions.a: A folk song recorded from village elders
o: A folk song recorded from village elders
Burnt grains from an ancient hearth
Animal teeth found in a buried pit
Bricks from a buried house wall

questions.q:
A historian has a heap of broken pots from an old site but no writing at all.
(a) Name two kinds of scientific study, mentioned in the chapter, that have added to history in the last 50 years or so.
(b) Which of them could tell her something more from the pots themselves, and why?
questions.a: (a) Any two of: studies of ancient climates, chemical studies of excavated materials, studies of the genetics of ancient people. (b) Chemical studies of excavated materials, because the pots are excavated materials; genetics studies need remains of people and climate studies tell about the weather, not the pots.
s: (a) Two of: ancient climates, chemical studies of excavated materials, genetics of ancient people
(b) Chemical studies, with the reason that the pots are excavated material

questions.q:
Assertion (A): An anthropologist could study the customs of a tribal community living today as well as the customs of a community from long ago.
Reason (R): Anthropologists study human societies and cultures from the oldest times to the present.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: True or False? 'A palaeontologist is the right specialist to study the bricks of a house wall buried 3,000 years ago.' Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. Parts of houses and bricks are remains that people left behind, which archaeologists dig up and study. Palaeontologists study fossil remains of plants, animals and humans from millions of years ago.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: bricks and house parts are studied by archaeologists; palaeontologists study fossils

questions.q: A district museum is planning an exhibition called 'What the people of our district made, and how they lived together, 2,000 years ago'. It has room for only two specialist corners, but four specialists have offered help: a geologist, a palaeontologist, an anthropologist and an archaeologist. Compare what each of the four studies, decide which two to leave out, and justify the choice using both halves of the exhibition's title.
questions.a: Geologist: the physical features of the Earth, such as soil, stones, hills and rivers; this is the land, not what the people made or how they lived. Palaeontologist: remains of plants, animals and humans from millions of years ago, preserved as fossils; far older than 2,000 years. Anthropologist: human societies and cultures from the oldest times to the present; this answers 'how they lived together'. Archaeologist: remains people left behind and that are dug up, such as tools, pots, beads, figurines and burnt grains; this answers 'what the people made'. Decision: leave out the geologist and the palaeontologist, since neither studies what the district's people made or how they lived together 2,000 years ago, while the archaeologist and the anthropologist each cover one half of the title.
s: Geologist: Earth's physical features, not people's making or living
Palaeontologist: fossils from millions of years ago
Anthropologist: human societies and cultures, matched to 'how they lived together'
Archaeologist: dug-up remains people left, matched to 'what they made'
Leaves out the geologist and the palaeontologist, justified from the title

questions.q: Four questions are asked about a hill village. Which one is a geologist best placed to answer?
questions.a: How the hill's soil and stone layers came to lie as they do
o: How the hill's soil and stone layers came to lie as they do
What the people of the village ate 2,000 years ago
What festivals the village community celebrates today
What the writing on a coin found in the village says

questions.q:
Scientists compare the skeletons from two old burials in the same valley, one about 600 years older than the other, to see whether certain features were passed down from the earlier group to the later one.
(a) Which kind of scientific study named in the chapter is this?
(b) Give one thing this study could tell a historian that a pot from the same burial could not.
questions.a: (a) A study of the genetics of ancient people (genetics studies how features get passed down from one generation to the next). (b) Whether the later people were descended from, or related to, the earlier ones; a pot tells what people made and used, not whose features were passed down to whom.
s: (a) A study of the genetics of ancient people
(b) Whether features were passed down / the groups were related, which a pot cannot show

questions.q:
Read the statements about who helps us learn about the past.
1. Epigraphists add to history by studying ancient inscriptions.
2. Newspapers become a useful source mainly when historians study recent history.
3. Chemical studies of excavated materials have been adding to history for more than 500 years.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 only
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
While trekking, Anil finds the impression of a leaf preserved in a layer of rock. At an old village site nearby, his sister finds a small clay toy in the soil.
(a) What is Anil's find called, and which specialist studies such finds?
(b) Why would an archaeologist, not that specialist, study the clay toy?
questions.a: (a) A fossil; palaeontologists study remains of plants, animals and humans from millions of years ago in the form of fossils. (b) The toy is something people made and left behind; archaeologists study such remains (tools, pots, beads, figurines, toys), not fossils of living things.
s: (a) Fossil, studied by a palaeontologist
(b) The toy is a remain left behind by people, which is the archaeologist's evidence

questions.q: Riya writes in her notebook: 'History is studied only by historians reading old books.' Which point from the chapter best corrects her?
questions.a: Archaeologists, epigraphists and scientists also add to it
o: Archaeologists, epigraphists and scientists also add to it
Historians study only the last two or three centuries of the past
Geologists study only the customs of the societies living today
Old books are never used as sources of history by anyone

questions.q: Write a short situation in which a palaeontologist, an archaeologist and an epigraphist all work on finds from the same hillside. Say what each one studies there.
questions.a: Example: Road builders cut into a hillside near Bhopal. In the deepest rock layer they find the impression of an ancient fish, which a palaeontologist studies as a fossil. Higher up, in the soil, they find pots, beads and a buried hearth, which an archaeologist digs up and studies as remains left by people. Among the pots lies a copper plate with writing on it, which an epigraphist reads because it is an ancient inscription.
s: Palaeontologist given a fossil to study
Archaeologist given remains left by people (pots, beads, tools, bricks)
Epigraphist given an ancient inscription

questions.q:
Read this report from a local newspaper.
'Scientists working with an excavation team have tested teeth from a 4,000-year-old burial to find which substances were present in them, and have found signs that the people ate millet. Another group, studying tiny plant remains in the soil layers, says the weather of the region was wetter then. "These studies mean we will not need diggers at old sites any more," said one visitor.'
(a) Which kind of scientific study, named in the chapter, was done on the teeth?
(b) Which kind of study named in the chapter does the second group's work belong to?
(c) About how long have such scientific studies been adding to history, according to the chapter?
(d) Is the visitor's remark right? Judge it using the report itself and the chapter.
questions.a: (a) A chemical study of excavated materials. (b) A study of ancient climates. (c) About the last 50 years. (d) No. The teeth tested came from an excavation, so the scientists depended on the diggers; the chapter says these studies supplement the more usual sources, they do not replace them.
s: (a) Chemical study of excavated materials
(b) Study of ancient climates
(c) The last 50 years or so
(d) No: the teeth came from a dig, and science supplements, not replaces, the usual sources

questions.q: The chapter asks, 'Can we compare historians to detectives?' Give your verdict and justify it with points from the chapter. (Either verdict earns the marks if it is reasoned from the chapter.)
questions.a: Yes, in several ways (a reasoned 'No', for example that a historian cannot question living witnesses about a king of 1,500 years ago, earns the same marks if it uses these chapter points). (1) A detective collects clues; a historian gathers information from as many sources as she can find and consult (objects, structures, texts, people). (2) Clues are like jigsaw pieces: sometimes sources confirm each other, the pieces match. (3) Sometimes sources contradict each other, and like a detective weighing witnesses, the historian must decide which source to trust more. (4) Some pieces of the puzzle remain missing, so she must work with gaps, as a detective often does. (5) From the pieces she tries to re-create the history of the period, as a detective re-creates what happened; she also takes help from experts (archaeologists, epigraphists, scientists) as a detective takes help from specialists.
s: Collecting clues: gathers information from as many sources as possible (either verdict, if reasoned)
Sources that confirm each other, like matching jigsaw pieces
Contradictory sources: decides which to trust more
Missing pieces: works with gaps in the evidence
Reconstructs the period, with help from other experts

questions.q:
A calendar-printing press keeps a record of the years for which it printed 366-day calendars. Its old ledger lists: 1888, 1892, 1896, 1904, 1908. A new worker notices that 1900 is missing and thinks a page has been lost.
(a) Using the Gregorian rule, explain why 1900 is missing.
(b) How many years passed between the two leap years 1896 and 1904?
(c) A customer brings in a 366-day calendar from a century year between 1500 and 1999. Which year must it be?
(d) The press has orders for 366-day calendars for 2096 and for 2100. Which order should it question before printing, and why?
questions.a: (a) Century years are leap years only if they are multiples of 400; 1900 is not (1900 / 400 = 4.75), so it had 365 days. (b) 8 years. (c) 1600, the only multiple of 400 in that range. (d) The order for 2100: it is a century year and not a multiple of 400 (2100 / 400 = 5.25), so it will have 365 days; 2096 is a multiple of 4 and not a century year, so it is a leap year.
s: (a) 1900 is a century year that is not a multiple of 400
(b) 8 years
(d) Question 2100, with the century-year reason

questions.q: An old museum card reads: 'Copper plate, AD 75. Coin, 75 BC.' The museum is rewriting its cards with the terms now used across the world. Which pair is correct?
questions.a: 75 CE for the plate and 75 BCE for the coin
o: 75 CE for the plate and 75 BCE for the coin
75 BCE for the plate and 75 CE for the coin
75 CE for the plate and 75 CE for the coin
75 BCE for the plate and 75 BCE for the coin

questions.q: Neha says: 'If two dates are both marked BCE, I can tell which one is earlier just from the numbers, without drawing a timeline.' Is she right? Explain with an example.
questions.a: Yes. BCE years are counted backward from the conventional year of Jesus' birth, so the larger the BCE number, the further back in time it is. For example, 560 BCE is earlier than 300 BCE. She only has to remember that this is the opposite of CE, where the larger number is later.
s: Verdict: yes, she is right
Reason: BCE years are counted backward, so the larger number is earlier
Correct example such as 560 BCE before 300 BCE

questions.q:
Read the statements about the way years are counted.
1. 'AD' and 'CE' label the same years; only the name has changed.
2. An era is the name for any period of exactly 100 years.
3. Calendars such as the Hindu, Muslim, Jewish and Chinese ones are still used to fix the dates of festivals.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: A copper plate is dated 'in the 12th year of King Vira's reign'. Another source shows that his reign began in 1110 CE, which counts as the 1st year of the reign. In which year was the plate issued?

A temple inscription gives its date only as 'year 35 of King Mahendrasena's reign' (an imaginary king).
(a) Using the chapter, explain why the people who carved it counted years this way instead of using CE.
(b) What one extra fact must a historian find before she can give the inscription a CE date, and why is that fact needed?
questions.a: (a) Each society and culture has had its own ways of measuring time, and the start of a ruler's reign has often marked the beginning of a new era; so they counted from the king's crowning. (b) The CE year in which the king's reign began: the inscription's count starts from his crowning, not from the conventional year of Jesus' birth, so without that year the 35 cannot be placed on the Gregorian count.
s: (a) Own way of measuring time: a ruler's reign marks a new era
(b) Needs the CE year of the reign's start, because the count begins at the crowning

questions.q: Suppose a scholar showed that Jesus was really born a few years away from the year generally taken for his birth. Would 1947 CE still be the right date for India's independence?
questions.a: Yes: the count starts from the conventional year, not a new one
o: Yes: the count starts from the conventional year, not a new one
No, because every CE date would then have to be renumbered at once
No, because the count would then have to start from the Buddha's birth
Yes, because CE years are counted backward from the year 1947 itself

questions.q: A shopkeeper sells a 'genuine ancient coin' with '45 BCE' stamped on it, saying it was stamped in the year it was made. Take it that people living in 45 BCE could not know when the starting point of the count (the conventional year of Jesus' birth) would come. Show that the shopkeeper's story cannot be true, using the chapter.
questions.a: BCE years are counted backward from the conventional year of Jesus' birth, so a BCE label can only be given by someone who already knows where that starting point lies. Either route then proves it (both earn full marks): (1) in 45 BCE the starting point was still 45 years in the future and unknown, so nobody could call that year '45 before' it; or (2) the chapter says each society has had its own ways of measuring time, so the coin's makers would have dated it in their own count, not in BCE. Either way, the '45 BCE' stamp must have been put on much later, so the coin is not what the shopkeeper says.
s: BCE counts backward from the conventional year of Jesus' birth
Either route: the starting point was unknown in 45 BCE, or societies used their own counts
Conclusion: the stamp (or coin) must be a later make

questions.q: Which list puts these years in order from the earliest to the latest?
questions.a: 560 BCE, 2 BCE, 300 CE, 1947 CE
o: 560 BCE, 2 BCE, 300 CE, 1947 CE
2 BCE, 560 BCE, 300 CE, 1947 CE
560 BCE, 300 CE, 2 BCE, 1947 CE
2 BCE, 300 CE, 560 BCE, 1947 CE

questions.q:
A heritage town's old tourist brochure says: 'Our stupa was built in 200 BC and our temple in 1150 AD. Our town also keeps its own calendar, counted from the crowning of its first king.' The tourism board is now putting up small stone signs at the gates of both buildings. Each sign has room for the date in only ONE system: either the town's own calendar, which local pilgrims use, or the labels used across the world. Most visitors now come from many countries.
(a) Rewrite the two dates with the labels now used across the world.
(b) Which building is older, and how can you tell from the labels alone?
(c) How many years before the temple was the stupa built? (There is no year zero.)
(d) Decide which system the signs should use, say whom your choice serves and what is lost by it. Either system is accepted if both are given.
questions.a: (a) 200 BCE and 1150 CE. (b) The stupa: a BCE date lies before the starting point of the count and every CE date after it. (c) 200 + 1150 - 1 = 1,349 years. (d) Either choice with its reason and loss. BCE/CE: the Gregorian calendar is commonly used worldwide, so visitors from many countries can read the dates; lost is the town's own count, the one its pilgrims use. Or the town's calendar: it keeps the era of the first king that local pilgrims use, as other calendars are still used side by side with the Gregorian one; lost is a date most foreign visitors can read. (The other system can go in the brochure.)
s: (a) 200 BCE and 1150 CE
(b) The stupa, because BCE dates come before all CE dates
(c) 1,349 years
(d) Either system, naming whom it serves and what is lost

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A calendar printed for 2000 showed 29 February, but a calendar printed for 1900 did not.
Reason (R): The Gregorian calendar has a leap year every four years.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
An office in Hyderabad prints its yearly holiday list with Gregorian dates, but the dates of Diwali and Eid change from year to year on that list.
(a) Which statement in the chapter explains why these festival dates move about?
(b) Why would the office still keep the Gregorian calendar for its work with other countries?
questions.a: (a) Side by side with the Gregorian calendar, Hindu, Muslim and other calendars are used for calculating the dates of festivals and auspicious events, so the festival dates are fixed by those calendars, not by the Gregorian one. (b) The Gregorian calendar is commonly used worldwide, so dates in it are understood everywhere.
s: (a) Festivals are dated by other calendars used side by side with the Gregorian
(b) The Gregorian calendar is the one commonly used worldwide

questions.q: A seal found at a site is dated 300 BCE and a coin from the same site 120 BCE. Since BCE years are counted backward, the seal is older than the coin by ___ years.

A small museum still uses old cards: 'Seal, 2600 BC'; 'Coin, AD 1835'; 'Statue, 150 BC'; 'Copper plate, AD 610'.
(a) Rewrite all four dates with the labels now used across the world.
(b) Arrange the four objects from the oldest to the newest.
(c) A visitor says the statue must be older than the seal because 150 is 'closer to the beginning of counting'. Explain his mistake.
(d) The museum will put the two objects made furthest apart in time side by side under a sign giving the gap between them. Which two objects, and what number of years should the sign give? (There is no year zero.)
questions.a: (a) Seal 2600 BCE; coin 1835 CE; statue 150 BCE; copper plate 610 CE. (b) Seal (2600 BCE), statue (150 BCE), copper plate (610 CE), coin (1835 CE). (c) BCE years are counted backward from the starting point, so 150 BCE, being nearer the starting point, is the more recent; 2600 BCE lies 2,450 years further back. (d) The seal and the coin: 2600 + 1835 - 1 = 4,434 years.
s: (a) All four rewritten with BCE and CE
(b) Correct order from oldest to newest
(c) Backward counting: 150 BCE is nearer the start and so more recent
(d) Seal and coin, 4,434 years apart

questions.q: True or False? 'An old museum card reads "Coin, 75 BC" and a new card in another museum reads "Coin, 75 BCE". The two coins must be from different years, because the labels differ.' Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. BC (Before Christ) is the older label and BCE (Before Common Era) the present one for the same years, counted backward from the conventional year of Jesus' birth. 75 BC and 75 BCE are the same year; only the name changed.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: BC is the old name for BCE, so both cards name the same year

questions.q: A kingdom decides to count its years afresh from the day its new queen is crowned. Which idea from the chapter does this follow?
questions.a: A ruler's reign starting has often begun a new era
o: A ruler's reign starting has often begun a new era
A century is the name for the years counted from a crowning
Years before the crowning must from now on be marked BCE
Every calendar must count its years from the birth of Jesus

questions.q:
A Gregorian year has 12 months adding up to 365 days, with a leap year every four years.
(a) A lighthouse keeper keeps one log page for every day from 1 January 2027 to 31 December 2029. How many pages does she fill?
(b) Her assistant says it must be 3 x 365 = 1,095 pages. What did he miss?
questions.a: (a) 365 + 366 + 365 = 1,096 pages. (b) 2028 is a leap year (a multiple of 4 that is not a century year), so it has 366 days; he counted every year as 365 days.
s: (a) 1,096 pages
(b) Missed that 2028 is a leap year of 366 days

questions.q:
Match each term in Column A with the description in Column B.
Column A: 1. AD  2. BCE  3. Era  4. Pañchānga
Column B: a. a distinct period of time, often begun by a major event  b. a book of tables listing the days of each month with astronomical data  c. the older label for years counted forward from the conventional birth of Jesus  d. the label now used for years counted backward from that point

Write a short situation in which one family in India uses the Gregorian calendar for one purpose and another calendar for a different purpose. Name both calendars and explain, using the chapter, why each one suits its purpose.
questions.a: Example: In Varanasi, Pooja's family books train tickets and notes her school exam dates using the Gregorian calendar, because it is commonly used worldwide and railways and schools all follow it. Her grandmother fixes the day of the Diwali puja from the Hindu calendar, because such calendars are used side by side with the Gregorian one to calculate the dates of festivals and auspicious events.
s: A believable situation with two different purposes
Gregorian calendar matched to a purpose, with the reason that it is used worldwide
Another named calendar matched to festival or auspicious dates

questions.q: A historian writing the history of a temple town has three dated records: (i) a copper plate dated 'in the 20th year of King Vira's reign'; (ii) a temple register that fixes the yearly festival by the Hindu calendar; (iii) a newspaper report dated 1950 CE. Explain, with five points from the chapter, why she meets more than one way of counting time here, and how she would bring all three records onto one Gregorian timeline for her readers.
questions.a: (1) Each society and culture has had its own ways of measuring time, so old records do not all use one count. (2) The start of a ruler's reign has often marked a new era: the copper plate counts from Vira's crowning, so she needs the CE year in which his reign began (year 20 is that year plus 19). (3) Hindu, Muslim, Jewish, Chinese and other calendars are used side by side with the Gregorian one to fix festivals: the register's festival dates must be turned into Gregorian dates. (4) The Gregorian calendar is commonly used worldwide, so readers anywhere will understand dates given in it; the newspaper already uses it. (5) In it, years after the starting point are CE and years before it BCE, so she labels every converted date CE or BCE and arranges them in order.
s: Each society has its own ways of measuring time
Reign-based era: needs the CE year of the reign's start
Festival calendars used side by side must be converted
Gregorian used worldwide, so it suits her readers
Labels all dates CE/BCE and orders them

questions.q:
Ravi says: 'The Gregorian calendar belongs only to the West, so the rest of the world does not use it.'
(a) Is Ravi right? Use what the chapter says about how widely the calendar and its labels are used.
(b) Ravi's aunt in Hyderabad fixes the date of Diwali by the Hindu calendar but dates her office letters in CE. Does this support or weaken Ravi's claim? Explain.
questions.a: (a) No. The chapter says the Gregorian calendar is commonly used worldwide, and its label CE (Common Era) is now used across the world. (b) It weakens the claim: she lives outside the West yet uses the Gregorian calendar for everyday dates, while using the Hindu calendar side by side for a festival, just as the chapter describes.
s: (a) No: commonly used worldwide, CE used across the world
(b) Weakens it: Gregorian for daily dates, another calendar side by side for festivals

questions.q:
In an inter-school quiz the question was: 'How many years passed from 75 BCE to 125 CE?' The answer sheets read:
Team Godavari: 200 years
Team Krishna: 199 years
Team Tungabhadra: 50 years
The quiz master can award the mark to only one team.
(a) Which team should get the mark?
(b) Show the working that supports your choice.
(c) What mistake did Team Tungabhadra make?
(d) What did Team Godavari forget, and how could a short timeline have helped them?
questions.a: (a) Team Krishna. (b) 75 + 125 - 1 = 199 years, since one date is BCE and the other CE. (c) They subtracted the numbers, 125 - 75 = 50, as if both dates were on the same side of the starting point. (d) They added correctly but forgot to subtract 1. Write the museum's reply: compare how centuries and millenniums are counted on the CE and the BCE sides of the starting point, and explain why the boundary years end in 01 and 00 on one side but the other way round on the other.
questions.a: (1) A century is any period of 100 years and a millennium any period of 1,000 years. (2) On the CE side they are counted forward starting from 1 CE: the 21st century CE runs from 2001 to 2100, and the 3rd millennium CE from 2001 to 3000. (3) On the BCE side they are counted from 1 BCE going back in time: the 3rd century BCE includes 300 BCE to 201 BCE and the 1st millennium BCE 1 BCE to 1000 BCE; so none of the boards is a mistake. (4) Because there is no year zero, the first block on each side starts at year 1, so a CE block starts at a year ending in 01 and ends at one ending in 00. (5) On the BCE side, read forward in time, a block starts at the year ending in 00 (300 BCE) and ends at the one ending in 01 (201 BCE): the mirror image of CE, which is why the boards seem to 'run backwards'.
s: Definitions of century and millennium
CE counting forward from 1 CE with an example
BCE counting backward from 1 BCE; boards are correct
No year zero, so each side starts at year 1
Explains the mirror pattern of 01/00 boundaries

s: Verdict: True
Reason: panels and sculptures are both Artistic Sources; a panel is not a Structure

questions.q: In her village, Lata records three things for a project: a copper plate with writing on it kept in the temple, a song about the village's founders sung by the elders, and a carved stone panel on the temple wall. How does the chapter group these three, in the same order?
questions.a: Archaeological, oral, artistic
o: Archaeological, oral, artistic
Literary, oral, archaeological
Archaeological, artistic, oral
Oral, literary, artistic

questions.q: Write a short situation in which a historian studying one village uses one archaeological source, one oral source and one artistic source, and each tells her something the other two cannot. Name the group (and sub-group, if archaeological) of each.
questions.a: Example: Studying the village of Kondapalli, a historian looks at pottery and toys dug from a mound (archaeological, Excavations), which show what people made and used; she listens to the genealogy a bard recites (oral), which gives the names of the families who led the village; and she studies a painting on the old temple wall (artistic), which shows how people dressed for a festival. Each adds a different piece of the picture.
s: An archaeological source with its sub-group and what it alone tells
An oral source and what it alone tells
An artistic source and what it alone tells

questions.q:
Match each find in Column A with its place in the chapter's chart of sources in Column B.
Column A: 1. A copper plate  2. A mound  3. Folklore  4. A sculpture
Column B: a. Oral source  b. Artistic source  c. Archaeological source: Inscriptions  d. Archaeological source: Structures

Rohan says: 'Folklore cannot be a source of history, because nobody wrote it down.'
(a) Where does the chapter place folklore?
(b) Use the chapter's definition of a source to show why being unwritten does not stop it from being one.
questions.a: (a) Among oral sources, along with genealogical accounts. (b) A source of history is a place, person, text or object from which we gather information about the past. A person telling a story passed down is such a source; writing is not required.
s: (a) Oral sources
(b) The definition includes a person, so writing is not needed

questions.q: A student sorting picture cards under 'Excavations' puts in pottery, figurines, a burial and a copper plate that was dug out of a mound, saying: 'Everything dug up goes here.' By the chapter's chart, which card is she wrong about?
questions.a: The copper plate: the chart lists it under Inscriptions
o: The copper plate: the chart lists it under Inscriptions
The burial: the chart lists burials under Structures
The figurines: the chart lists them under Artistic sources
The pottery: the chart lists pots under Inscriptions

questions.q:
A historian is studying a queen who ruled about 1,500 years ago. She has four sources: (i) a copper plate recording a land grant in the queen's name; (ii) a carved panel showing the queen's court; (iii) a folk tale saying the queen ruled for 40 years; (iv) coins bearing the queen's name.
(a) Classify each of the four sources.
(b) Which two sources belong to the same sub-group?
(c) The copper plate and the coins suggest a reign of about 15 years. What does this mean for the folk tale?
(d) What should the historian do before writing her account?
questions.a: (a) (i) archaeological, inscription; (ii) artistic, panel; (iii) oral, folklore; (iv) archaeological, inscription. (b) The copper plate and the coins, both Inscriptions. (c) The folk tale contradicts two sources that confirm each other, so the jigsaw pieces do not match; she must decide which source she can trust more. (d) Gather as many further sources as she can find and consult before deciding, since pieces may be missing.
s: (a) All four classified correctly
(b) Copper plate and coins: Inscriptions
(c) The folk tale contradicts two sources that confirm each other, so she must decide which to trust more
(d) Consult as many more sources as possible before deciding

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Coins are counted among the archaeological sources of history.
Reason (R): Historians sometimes find that their sources give contradictory information.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q:
A historian studying a river town uses four things: a ruined fort, an old boatman who tells the songs his grandfather taught him, a diary written in 1890, and an iron sword.
(a) The chapter defines a source of history as 'a place, person, text or object'. Match each of the four to one word of that definition.
(b) Which of the four would an archaeologist most likely have dug up, and under which sub-group of the chart would it go?
questions.a: (a) The fort is a place, the boatman a person, the diary a text and the sword an object. (b) The sword: Archaeological Sources, Excavations (tools and weapons).
s: (a) Fort-place, boatman-person, diary-text, sword-object
(b) The sword, under Excavations (tools and weapons)

questions.q:
A painting on an old temple wall and a song sung in the same village both describe a battle.
(a) Classify the two sources using the chapter's chart.
(b) A low mound outside the village is said to be the battle camp. Under which group and sub-group does the mound fall?
questions.a: (a) The painting is an artistic source; the song is an oral source (folklore). (b) Archaeological Sources, Structures (mounds and monuments).
s: (a) Painting: artistic; song: oral (folklore)
(b) Mound: Archaeological, Structures

questions.q:
A coin was found when archaeologists dug into an old settlement. Rahul says: 'Since it was dug up, the chart must place it under Excavations, not Inscriptions.'
(a) Where does the chapter's chart place coins?
(b) Give the clue from the chart's lists that settles where a dug-up coin goes.
questions.a: (a) Under Archaeological Sources, Inscriptions (with manuscripts and copper plates). (b) The chart lists coins by name under Inscriptions, and its Excavations list (remains, tools and weapons, figurines and ornaments, pottery and toys, habitations and burials) does not include coins; so a coin goes under Inscriptions even if it was dug up.
s: (a) Inscriptions
(b) Coins are listed under Inscriptions and not in the Excavations list

questions.q: Ira claims: 'A source is useful to a historian only when it agrees with the other sources.' Is Ira right? Explain using the chapter's jigsaw idea.
questions.a: No. Historians gather information from as many sources as they can. Sometimes the sources confirm each other, like matching jigsaw pieces; at other times they give contradictory information, like pieces that do not match. A source that disagrees is not thrown away: the historian must then decide which source can be trusted more, and that judgement is part of how she re-creates the history of the period.
s: Verdict: no
Sources may confirm or contradict, like matching or non-matching jigsaw pieces
A contradicting source still matters: the historian decides which to trust more

questions.q: A museum storeroom holds: a burial with pots, a clay figurine, a coin, a genealogy of a ruling family recited by a bard, a carved stone panel and a mound photographed from the air. Sort all six into the chapter's groups, giving the sub-group for the archaeological ones.
questions.a: Archaeological, Excavations: the burial with pots, the figurine. Archaeological, Inscriptions: the coin. Archaeological, Structures: the mound. Oral: the genealogy. Artistic: the stone panel.
s: Excavations: burial and figurine
Inscriptions: coin; Structures: mound
Oral: genealogy; Artistic: panel

questions.q:
A school is writing the history of its 100-year-old building. It has: (i) a copper plate set into the foundation, with lines of writing and the opening year engraved on it; (ii) the building itself; (iii) a painting of the opening day; (iv) the memories of a retired teacher who taught there for 30 years; (v) coins and broken pots dug up when the new hall's foundation was laid.
(a) Place each of the five in the chapter's chart, giving the sub-group for the archaeological ones.
(b) Which source is 'a person' in the chapter's definition of a source?
(c) Which source is best for the year the school opened, and which for what daily life there was like 30 years ago? Give a reason for each.
questions.a: (a) (i) Archaeological, Inscriptions (a copper plate); (ii) Archaeological, Structures: an old building counts as a monument-like structure, the only group of the chart that fits, and the chapter asks what old houses or buildings can tell us; (iii) Artistic (a painting); (iv) Oral (memories passed on by a person); (v) coins: Archaeological, Inscriptions; broken pots: Archaeological, Excavations (pottery). (b) The retired teacher. (c) The copper plate for the opening year, since its date was engraved at the time; the teacher's memories for daily life 30 years ago, since she lived and worked there then.
s: (a) Copper plate and coins: Inscriptions; building: Structures (a monument-like old building)
(a) Painting: Artistic; memories: Oral; pots: Excavations
(b) The retired teacher
(c) The copper plate for the opening year, with reason
(c) Teacher's memories for daily life, with reason

questions.q:
Read this note from a student's field diary.
'In Ramapuram the elders sing a ballad saying the village was set up by a chieftain's family who came from the coast. Outside the village is a low mound; when the state team dug into it, they found pottery and two burials. In the temple there is a copper plate recording a gift of land to the village.'
(a) In which group of sources does the ballad belong?
(b) The mound and the copper plate are both archaeological sources. Under which different sub-groups does the chapter place them?
(c) The historian wants to know what the people of the first settlement made and used. Which of the three sources is most useful for this, and why can the ballad not answer it?
questions.a: (a) Oral sources (folklore). (b) The mound is a Structure; the copper plate is an Inscription. (The pottery and burials dug from the mound are Excavations.) (c) The finds from the mound: the pottery and burials are remains the people themselves left behind, showing what they made and how they buried their dead. The ballad tells who founded the village and where they came from, not the objects they made and used.
s: (a) Oral source
(b) Mound: Structures; copper plate: Inscriptions
(c) Picks the mound finds as remains people left, and says why the ballad cannot answer

questions.q: A museum guide has made a chart of sources for visitors, but three of its lines are wrong: 'Coins - Excavations', 'Folklore - Artistic Sources' and 'Mounds - Excavations'. Correct the three lines, then compare the three groups archaeological, oral and artistic (with what each includes), and analyse why a historian studying an ancient monument would want sources from more than one group.
questions.a: Corrections: coins belong under Inscriptions (with manuscripts and copper plates); folklore is an Oral Source (with genealogical accounts); mounds are Structures (with monuments). Comparison: Archaeological Sources have three sub-groups, Inscriptions, Structures and Excavations (remains, tools and weapons, figurines and ornaments, pottery and toys, habitations and burials); Oral Sources are genealogical accounts and folklore; Artistic Sources are paintings, sculptures and panels. Analysis: the monument is only one piece; an inscription on it, finds dug up around it, panels carved on it and tales told about it each add a different piece, and historians gather information from as many sources as they can.
s: Coins corrected to Inscriptions
Folklore corrected to Oral; mounds to Structures
Archaeological sub-groups compared
Oral and Artistic groups with their members
Each group adds a different piece, so many sources are used

questions.q: A historian finds a very old text written in a language that few people read today. According to the chapter, whose help would she most need to make use of it?
questions.a: An expert in literature and languages
o: An expert in literature and languages
A geologist
A palaeontologist
An anthropologist studying a village today

questions.q: Kabir says: 'A travelogue by a foreign visitor 1,000 years ago is only one piece of the jigsaw. If a copper plate of the same king tells a different story, the historian should not simply believe the visitor because he was an outsider; she should decide which source she can trust more, and look for still more sources.' Is Kabir right? Explain using the chapter's chart and what it says about how historians work.
questions.a: Yes. The travelogue is a literary source (Foreign Accounts) and the copper plate an archaeological one (Inscriptions), so they are two different pieces. The chapter says that when sources give contradictory information (the jigsaw pieces don't match), historians need to decide which source they can trust more, and that they gather information from as many sources as they can find; it gives no rule that a foreign account wins.
s: Verdict: yes
Travelogue: Foreign Accounts; copper plate: Inscriptions
Pieces that don't match: decide which to trust more, using as many sources as possible

questions.q:
Match each source in Column A with its place in the chapter's chart in Column B.
Column A: 1. A travelogue  2. Folklore  3. A copper plate  4. A play
Column B: a. Literary source: Foreign Accounts  b. Oral source  c. Archaeological source: Inscriptions  d. Literary source: Indian Literature

A bard recites from memory the line of kings of an old Indian kingdom. A historical text written at that kingdom's court lists the same kings in the same order.
(a) In which group of sources does each belong?
(b) What does the match tell the historian, in the chapter's jigsaw words, and why is that more useful than either source alone?
questions.a: (a) The bard's recital is an oral source (a genealogical account); the court text is a literary source (Indian Literature, a historical text). (b) The jigsaw pieces match: the two sources confirm each other. Coming from different groups, they back each other up, so the historian can trust the list more than she could trust either one alone.
s: (a) Oral (genealogical) and literary (historical text)
(b) The sources confirm each other, so the list is better supported

questions.q:
A school library has two history boxes, 'Indian Literature' and 'Foreign Accounts'. The teacher wants each type the chapter lists under a branch to be shown in its box. The 'Foreign Accounts' box already holds two travelogues and nothing else, and has room for only one more item. A new parcel holds:
W. A traveller's account of the markets of the Deccan, written by a visitor from across the sea
X. A book of plays written by an Indian poet
Y. An audio recording of village folk songs
Z. A foreign writer's historical chronicle of a king's reign
(a) Which box should X go into?
(b) Which two items are candidates for the 'Foreign Accounts' box, and what type is each?
(c) Why does Y fit neither box?
(d) Decide which candidate takes the last place, and say what is lost by leaving out the other.
questions.a: (a) Indian Literature (poems and plays). (b) W, a travelogue, and Z, a historical chronicle. (c) Folk songs are folklore, an oral source, not a literary one. (d) Z, the chronicle: the box already has travelogues but no historical chronicle, the other type listed under Foreign Accounts, so Z completes the box. Leaving out W loses a third visitor's view of the Deccan markets, but travelogues are already shown.
s: (a) Indian Literature
(b) W (travelogue) and Z (historical chronicle)
(c) Y is folklore, an oral source
(d) Chooses Z because chronicles are missing, and names the loss of W

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A historian who finds a travelogue written in a language few people read today may need the help of an expert in languages.
Reason (R): Experts in literature and languages work only with archaeological sources.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false.
o: A is true, but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: A historian has a travelogue by a visitor who spent one month at a king's court. Which question can this source NOT answer on its own?
questions.a: What the court was like in the years after the visitor left
o: What the court was like in the years after the visitor left
What the visitor noticed at the court during his stay
What goods he saw in the markets on his journey
Which towns he passed through on his way

questions.q: Write one question about the past that a historian could answer with a travelogue but not with a scientific and technological text, and one question for which it is the other way round. Explain, for each, why that source suits it.
questions.a: Example: (1) 'What did a visitor from another land notice about the clothes people wore in the markets of a Deccan town?' A travelogue (Foreign Accounts) records what a visitor saw on his journey; a scientific text does not describe such scenes. (2) 'How did people of that time work metals?' A scientific and technological text (Indian Literature) explains such methods; a traveller's account of his journey usually would not. A travelogue is a record of observation, a technical text a record of knowledge.
s: A question suited to a travelogue, with a reason
A question suited to a scientific and technological text, with a reason
Contrast of what each kind of text records

questions.q: A library has two books about an old Indian port: one written by a sailor from across the sea describing what he saw on his voyage, and a book of plays by a poet of the port itself. A student shelves both in one box 'because both are about the same port'. Which shelving follows the chapter's chart?
questions.a: Sailor's book: Foreign Accounts; plays: Indian Literature
o: Sailor's book: Foreign Accounts; plays: Indian Literature
Both in Indian Literature, since both are about an Indian port
Both in Foreign Accounts, since both describe a trading port
Sailor's book: Oral sources; plays: Artistic sources

questions.q:
A foreign writer's chronicle says a king ruled for 30 years. The king's own copper plates are dated across only 12 years of his reign.
(a) Place the two sources in the chapter's chart.
(b) Do the two sources necessarily contradict each other? Explain what the historian should do.
questions.a: (a) The chronicle: Literary Sources, Foreign Accounts (historical chronicle). The copper plates: Archaeological Sources, Inscriptions. (b) Not necessarily: plates from only 12 years may simply mean other plates are missing pieces of the puzzle. She should look for more sources (coins, other inscriptions, Indian texts) before deciding which account she can trust more.
s: (a) Chronicle: Foreign Accounts; plates: Inscriptions
(b) Gap may be missing pieces; consult more sources before deciding

questions.q:
Read the statements about literary sources.
1. The Vedas and Itihasas are listed under Foreign Accounts.
2. Historical chronicles are listed under Indian Literature only.
3. Poems and plays are counted among Literary Sources.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 3 only
o: 3 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
A historian has two translated texts about the same imaginary 12th-century Indian king: a historical text written at his own court, and a travelogue by a visitor from another land who spent one year in his kingdom. She wants to answer:
(i) Which towns did a traveller pass on the road to the capital?
(ii) In what order did the king's ancestors rule?
(iii) What did the markets look like in the year of the visit?
Place both texts in the chart. Then, for each question, say which text is better placed to answer it and why. Finally, name one source from a different group of the chart that could add to (iii), and say why historians look for it.
questions.a: Placing: the court text is Literary, Indian Literature (historical text); the travelogue is Literary, Foreign Accounts (travelogue). (i) The travelogue: it records the visitor's own journey to the capital. (ii) The court text: it is the kingdom's own record of the king and his line, while a visitor of one year saw only his own time. (iii) The travelogue, since the visitor saw the markets himself that year (the court text may add the kingdom's view). Another group: excavations at the market site (pottery, habitations) or coins (Inscriptions); historians gather information from as many sources as they can find, so other pieces can confirm or contradict the texts.
s: Both texts placed in the right branch and type
(i) Travelogue, the visitor's own journey
(ii) Court text, the kingdom's own record of its line
(iii) Travelogue, the visitor saw the markets that year
Names a source from another group (excavations or coins) and why many sources are used

questions.q: An ancient Indian text explains how to measure fields and how to work metals. Under which heading of the chart does it belong?
questions.a: Indian Literature: scientific and technological texts
o: Indian Literature: scientific and technological texts
Foreign Accounts: historical chronicles of distant lands
Indian Literature: poems and plays about the old crafts
Archaeological sources: Structures

questions.q:
An old Indian text explains, step by step, how to build a stepwell.
(a) Place it in the chapter's chart: group, branch and type.
(b) Why can this text not, by itself, tell a historian that such a stepwell was actually built in a particular town? Which kind of source could show that?
questions.a: (a) Literary Sources, Indian Literature, scientific and technological texts. (b) The text tells how a stepwell is built, not where one was built. The stepwell itself, or its remains, in that town would show it: an archaeological source (a Structure, or remains from an excavation).
s: (a) Literary, Indian Literature, scientific and technological text
(b) A how-to text does not prove a building existed; the structure or its remains would

questions.q:
A grandmother tells a folk tale about a clever minister. Later, the same tale is found printed in an old collection of stories.
(a) Into which group of sources does each version fall?
(b) Why are they placed in different groups though the story is the same?
questions.a: (a) The grandmother's telling is an oral source (folklore); the printed collection of stories is a literary source (Indian Literature). (b) The chapter defines a source as a place, person, text or object. The told version reaches us through a person, which the chart counts as oral; the printed version is a text, which the chart counts as literary.
s: (a) Oral (folklore) and literary (collection of stories)
(b) One comes through a person, the other is a text

questions.q: A teacher asks the class to bring examples of Literary Sources. Which of these examples should she NOT accept?
questions.a: A genealogy recited from memory by a bard
o: A genealogy recited from memory by a bard
A collection of stories
A historical chronicle by a foreign writer
A book of poems

questions.q: Sort these six texts into the two branches of Literary Sources, naming the type each one is in the chart: a collection of Vedic hymns, an epic of the Itihasa tradition, a play performed at court, a book on metal-working, a visitor's diary of his travels, and a foreign writer's record of a king's wars.
questions.a: Indian Literature: the Vedic hymns and the epic (Vedas and Itihasas), the court play (poems and plays), the metal-working book (scientific and technological texts). Foreign Accounts: the visitor's diary (travelogue) and the foreign writer's record of wars (historical chronicle).
s: Vedic hymns and epic: Vedas and Itihasas, Indian Literature
Play and metal-working book placed correctly in Indian Literature
Travelogue and historical chronicle under Foreign Accounts

questions.q:
Read these two extracts, both said to describe the same ancient city.
Extract 1, from a visitor who came from a distant land: 'The streets here are wide, and in the great market I saw heaps of cotton cloth and bright beads for sale.'
Extract 2, from a play written by an Indian poet of the same time: 'The heroine walks through the busy bazaar, past the sellers of cotton cloth.'
(a) Name the branch of Literary Sources and the type for Extract 1.
(b) Name the branch and the type for Extract 2.
(c) In the chapter's jigsaw language, what is happening when these two extracts are put side by side?
(d) A student argues that Extract 2 must be the more trustworthy one simply because it was written by an Indian. Judge this argument.
questions.a: (a) Foreign Accounts: a travelogue. (b) Indian Literature: poems and plays. (c) The pieces match: the two sources confirm each other about a cloth market. (d) The argument is weak. The chapter says historians decide which source to trust more when sources contradict, and here they agree; it gives no rule that a source is more trustworthy because of who wrote it. Both are counted as sources, and the historian checks them against each other and against other sources.
s: (a) Foreign Accounts: travelogue
(b) Indian Literature: poems and plays
(c) The sources confirm each other; the pieces match
(d) Rejects the argument: trust is judged by checking sources, not by the writer's origin

questions.q:
A historian studying an old port city has a chronicle written by a visitor in his own faraway language, and an Indian poem in an old language few people read today.
(a) Whom does the chapter name as able to help her read both?
(b) Why might she still want an archaeologist's help for the same city?
questions.a: (a) Experts in literature and languages. (b) The texts tell what their writers wrote down; an archaeologist digs up the remains people actually left in the city, such as pots, tools and parts of houses, which add pieces the texts may not have.
s: (a) Experts in literature and languages
(b) Archaeologists dig up remains that add pieces the texts may not give

questions.q:
A historian is writing about trade in an old port city. She has: (i) an Indian poem praising the city's ships; (ii) a foreign traveller's travelogue describing its markets; (iii) a scientific text on building ships; (iv) beads and pots dug up at the old harbour; (v) a folk song of fishermen about a great storm that no text mentions.
(a) Which of these are literary sources? Give the branch and type of each.
(b) Which source would show what goods were actually handled at the harbour, whatever writers said? Name its group.
(c) Why does she need both an expert in languages and an archaeologist?
(d) What does the folk song show about relying on literary sources alone?
questions.a: (a) The poem: Indian Literature (poems and plays); the travelogue: Foreign Accounts (travelogue); the shipbuilding text: Indian Literature (scientific and technological texts). (b) The beads and pots: Archaeological Sources (Excavations). (c) The texts must be read, some in old or foreign languages, which experts in literature and languages help with; the harbour finds must be dug up and studied, which is the archaeologist's work. (d) The storm is remembered only in an oral source, so texts alone would leave a gap; some pieces of the puzzle can be missing from any one group, so historians consult as many sources as they can.
s: (a) Poem and shipbuilding text: Indian Literature (types); travelogue: Foreign Accounts
(b) Beads and pots: Archaeological (Excavations)
(c) Language expert for texts, archaeologist for dug-up finds
(d) Texts alone leave gaps; oral sources fill some

questions.q: In a rock shelter, a team finds stone blades, arrowheads, a pendant made of animal teeth and ash from old fires, but no pots and no metal. Which way of life do these finds fit best?
questions.a: Hunter-gatherers using fire and stone tools
o: Hunter-gatherers using fire and stone tools
A farming village that sowed its fields together
A small town trading in copper tools with villages
A settled village exchanging iron ornaments

questions.q: True or False? 'Early humans made ornaments only for their own use and never passed them on to other groups.' Give the verdict and the reason or the correction.
questions.a: False. Early humans learned to make simple ornaments such as stone or shell beads and pendants of animal teeth, and they sometimes exchanged them with other groups.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: ornaments were sometimes exchanged with other groups

questions.q: Which of these finds would most surprise an archaeologist digging a rock shelter of early hunter-gatherers, before any farming began?
questions.a: An iron ploughshare
o: An iron ploughshare
A pendant of animal teeth
Ash from an old fire
Stone arrowheads

questions.q:
Read the statements about early communities.
1. In early farming communities, each family owned its own piece of land.
2. Copper came into use before iron.
3. Early hunter-gatherer bands lived mainly in permanent houses of brick.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 only
o: 2 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1 only

questions.q: Taking the last Ice Age to have begun 100,000 years ago and to have ended around 12,000 years ago, it lasted about ___ thousand years.

A student says: 'We cannot read anything early humans said or wrote, so we know nothing about how they lived.'
(a) Which part of his statement fits what the chapter says about their languages, and what kind of source does that leave us without?
(b) Name two kinds of evidence from the chapter that show the second part is wrong.
questions.a: (a) The first part fits: the chapter says they communicated using languages that are now lost, so we have no records, writings or tales in their own words (accept any of these). (b) Rock paintings found in hundreds of caves, and objects they made such as improved stone axes, blades and arrowheads (or ornaments such as beads).
s: (a) First part fits: languages lost, so no records or tales in their own words
(b) Rock paintings and objects such as stone tools or ornaments

questions.q:
After the Ice Age, a group with cattle, goats and seed grain is choosing where to live.
Site A: a gentle slope a ten-minute walk above the river, safe from floods, with fair soil.
Site B: the river bank itself, with water close by and soft, rich soil; old flood marks show the water has reached this bank in some years.
Site C: a cave in a forest, good for shelter and for hunting deer.
(a) Which site matches the way of life the group is leaving behind?
(b) What two things does Site B offer that the chapter says drew farming groups to rivers?
(c) What does the chapter's account of the melting ice suggest about why rivers like this one could flood?
(d) One member says: 'The Ice Age is over, so the old flood marks on Site B do not matter any more.' Using your answer to (c), explain why he is wrong, and suggest one way the group could still use Site B's soil while keeping its huts safe.
questions.a: (a) Site C: a cave for shelter and hunting suits hunter-gatherers. (b) Water close at hand, and more fertile soil that makes growing crops easier. (c) When the climate warmed, the melting ice sent waters that swelled the existing rivers, so their banks could be flooded. (d) He is wrong because the floods come from the warming after the Ice Age, not from the Ice Age itself: the melted ice swelled the rivers. Any sensible plan is accepted, for example building the huts on Site A, above the flood marks, and farming the river bank below.
s: (a) Site C
(b) Water and fertile soil
(c) Melting ice swelled the rivers
(d) Floods came from the warming after the Ice Age, plus a plan that keeps huts above the flood marks (e.g. huts on A, fields on B)

questions.q: After the Ice Age, a group with seeds of grain must choose between a dry hilltop with a wide view and the bank of a river. Which reason from the chapter favours the river bank?
questions.a: Water was at hand and the soil was more fertile
o: Water was at hand and the soil was more fertile
Rivers kept away the cold of the Ice Age in winter
Copper could be found only along the banks of rivers
Rock shelters were found only beside flowing rivers

questions.q:
Early bands sometimes exchanged ornaments with other groups. Later, villages exchanged food, clothing and tools.
(a) What changed in the kind of goods being exchanged?
(b) Using the chapter, give one reason why farming villages had more of such goods to exchange.
questions.a: (a) From occasional ornaments (beads, pendants) to everyday goods: mostly food, clothing and tools. (b) With cultivation and domesticated animals more food was available, communities grew in size and number, and settled villages built up networks of exchange.
s: (a) From ornaments to everyday goods (food, clothing, tools)
(b) More food and larger settled communities with exchange networks

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Early farming communities often settled near rivers.
Reason (R): Early humans used fire and made improved stone tools such as axes and blades.
Choose the correct option.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.q: Interpret why the chapter says that, as communities grew, 'so did their social complexity'. Give three features of the way these communities were run.
questions.a: (1) Leaders or chieftains were responsible for the well-being of the people. (2) Everyone worked collectively towards the community's welfare. (3) There was no sense of individual ownership: the lands were sowed and harvested collectively. Larger groups needed such leaders and shared ways of working, which a small band did not.
s: Chieftains responsible for people's well-being
Everyone worked together for the community's welfare
No individual ownership; lands sown and harvested collectively

questions.q:
A museum wants four panels in the right order of time:
P. Hamlets grow into villages that exchange food, clothing and tools
Q. Bands of hunter-gatherers live in caves and rock shelters
R. Some villages, linked by networks of exchange, grow into small towns
S. After the Ice Age, groups settle down and cultivate cereals
Which order is correct?
questions.a: Q, S, P, R
o: Q, S, P, R
S, Q, P, R
Q, P, S, R
Q, S, R, P

questions.q:
Three settlements lie in a valley. Kanu has twelve huts and grows millet. Pala is a sizeable village that swaps grain for cloth and tools with its neighbours. Teja is joined by paths to several villages, and people from all of them come there to exchange goods and news.
(a) Which settlement is a hamlet, and which is the most likely to grow into a small town?
(b) What, according to the chapter, turned some villages into small towns?
questions.a: (a) Kanu is the hamlet (a small settlement); Teja is the most likely to become a small town. (b) Networks of communication and exchange were established among villages, and some of those villages grew into small towns.
s: (a) Kanu the hamlet; Teja the likely town
(b) Networks of communication and exchange among villages

questions.q: A team finds shell beads both in a rock shelter and in an early farming village. A trainee concludes that the two sites must be from the same time. Compare the life of early hunter-gatherers with that of early farming communities under four heads (shelter, food, tools and technology, how the group was run), and then judge the trainee's conclusion.
questions.a: (1) Shelter: hunter-gatherers lived in temporary camps, rock shelters or caves; farmers settled down, often near rivers, in hamlets and villages. (2) Food: hunting and collecting edible plants and fruits, against cultivating cereals and grains and keeping cattle and goats. (3) Tools: fire and stone tools such as axes, blades and arrowheads, against pottery and metal (copper first, iron later) for durable tools. (4) Running the group: bands helping each other, against chieftains responsible for well-being, collective work and no individual ownership of land. (5) Judgement: the conclusion does not follow. Hunter-gatherers made stone or shell beads and farming people also made ornaments, so beads alone cannot date a site; the other finds, such as stone tools against pots, fields or metal, must decide it.
s: Shelter compared
Food compared
Tools and technology compared
How the group was run compared
Rejects the conclusion: beads were made in both ways of life, other finds decide

questions.q:
A group lives in a cave. In spring its members collect berries and roots, in winter they hunt deer, and they move to a new camp whenever food runs short.
(a) An archaeologist digs at one of the group's old camps and expects to find pots and stored grain. Is she likely to? Use the chapter's term for this way of life in your answer.
(b) Why would a band of 25 people be more likely to survive than one family living alone?
questions.a: (a) Unlikely: they are hunter-gatherers who lived in temporary camps, rock shelters or caves and moved on when food ran short; pottery and stored cereals came with settled farming communities. (b) Early humans faced many challenges from nature and lived in bands or groups to help each other while seeking food and shelter.
s: (a) Unlikely: hunter-gatherers in temporary camps; pots and grain came with settled farmers
(b) Bands helped each other against nature's challenges

questions.q: Which find would best tell an archaeologist that the people of a settlement had begun to domesticate animals?
questions.a: Goat and cattle bones beside huts, with stored grain
o: Goat and cattle bones beside huts, with stored grain
Stone arrowheads lying next to the bones of wild deer
A rock painting of hunters chasing a large herd of deer
A pendant made from the teeth of a wild animal

questions.q: Aman says: 'Early humans spent all their time searching for food, so they could not have had any art or beliefs.' Is Aman right? Give evidence from the chapter.
questions.a: No. Early humans did constantly seek shelter and food, but they also made rock paintings, found in hundreds of caves all over the world, some showing simple figures or symbols and others detailed scenes with animals or humans. They made ornaments such as beads and pendants. And the chapter says they had certain beliefs about the natural elements and possibly some notion of an afterlife.
s: Verdict: no
Evidence of art: rock paintings and ornaments
Evidence of beliefs: natural elements and possibly an afterlife

questions.q:
A museum panel reads: 'Homo sapiens: about 300,000 years. End of the last Ice Age: around 12,000 years ago; settling and farming began afterwards, taken here as about 12,000 years ago.' Take the present year as 2026 CE.
(a) Turn '12,000 years ago' into a date.
(b) For about how many years did Homo sapiens live before settling and farming began?
(c) What percentage of the whole 300,000 years is that?
(d) A visitor writes in the comment book: 'Farming has been part of human life for most of our history.' Judge the comment using your answers.
questions.a: (a) B + 2026 - 1 = 12,000, so about 9975 BCE. (b) 300,000 - 12,000 = 288,000 years. (c) 288,000 / 300,000 = about 96%. (d) The comment is wrong: for about 96% of our time as Homo sapiens, humans were hunter-gatherers; farming covers only roughly the last 12,000 years, about 4%.
s: (a) About 9975 BCE
(b) About 288,000 years
(c) About 96% (accept 96 to 97)
(d) Rejects the comment: farming is only about the last 4% of human time

questions.q:
A potter and a coppersmith settle in a growing village.
(a) What would each of them make, going by the chapter?
(b) Which advantage does the chapter link to tools made of metal?
questions.a: (a) The potter makes pots and other clay objects; the coppersmith makes tools, objects of daily use and ornaments of copper. (b) Metal helped make durable tools, objects and ornaments.
s: (a) Pots and clay objects; copper tools, objects and ornaments
(b) Metal made tools and objects durable

questions.q: Write a short scene set in a valley about 9,000 years ago that shows three different things the chapter says happened after the last Ice Age. After the scene, label each of the three.
questions.a: Example: In a small hamlet, people walk out together at dawn to sow barley in the shared field while a boy drives the goats and cattle to graze. The chieftain checks that every family has grain stored for the winter, and an old woman shapes clay pots by the fire. Labels: (1) cultivating cereals and grains, (2) domesticating animals such as goats and cattle, (3) social complexity: a chieftain responsible for well-being and collective sowing (pottery as a new technology is also accepted).
s: A first post-Ice Age change shown and labelled
A second change shown and labelled
A third change shown and labelled

questions.q: A classmate's poster says: 'Early humans had an easy life: plenty of space, no towns and nothing to worry about. In the end they settled in villages only because they got bored of moving.' Judge both parts of the poster, using three points from the chapter on the challenges early humans faced and two points on what actually made settling down possible and attractive.
questions.a: Part 1 is wrong. (1) Early humans faced many challenges from nature and had to live in bands or groups to help each other. (2) They were constantly seeking shelter and food, living in temporary camps, rock shelters or caves. (3) In an Ice Age it was very cold and much of the Earth was covered with ice; the last one lasted from over 100,000 to around 12,000 years ago. Part 2 is also wrong. (4) Only after the last Ice Age, when the climate warmed, did living conditions improve so that many groups started settling down, cultivating cereals and grains and domesticating animals. (5) With more food, communities grew and often settled near rivers, because of the water and the more fertile soil.
s: Challenges from nature; living in bands
Constant search for shelter and food
Ice Age cold over a very long period
Settling followed the warming after the last Ice Age, with crops and animals
Settled near rivers for water and fertile soil, not boredom

questions.q:
A described scene: Inside a rock shelter, a fire burns near the entrance. Two people chip stones into blades and arrowheads. On the rock wall, someone has painted a herd of deer being chased by figures with bows. A woman threads shell beads on a cord, and a visitor from another group hands over a pendant of animal teeth in return for some of her beads. There are no fields, pots or metal objects anywhere.
(a) How did this group most likely get its food? Give a clue from the scene.
(b) What does the bead-for-pendant handover show about such groups?
(c) For a historian today, what kind of source is the painted wall, in the chapter's chart?
(d) A student labels the scene 'an early farming village'. Judge the label, using two clues from the scene.
questions.a: (a) By hunting (and gathering): the arrowheads and the painted hunt of deer. (b) Early humans sometimes exchanged ornaments with other groups. (c) An artistic source (a painting). (d) The label is wrong. A farming village would have cultivated fields and, later, pots or metal tools; the scene has no fields, pots or metal, and the people live in a rock shelter and make stone tools, which fits hunter-gatherers.
s: (a) Hunting, with the arrowheads or painted hunt as the clue
(b) Groups sometimes exchanged ornaments
(c) Artistic source
(d) Rejects the label with two clues such as no fields, no pots, rock shelter, stone tools
